identifies unusual, incorrect, or atypical events. The output is a flag, 1 for an anomaly and 0 otherwise, or a probability of an anomaly. Supervised anomaly detection learns from examples labeled “normal” and “abnormal”. Unsupervised anomaly detection describes the normal behavior, for example with a density estimate, and flags the examples that deviate from it. Applications include credit card fraud detection, intrusion detection, removing outliers before a statistical analysis, change detection, system health monitoring, and fault detection.

produces new examples that resemble the training data: images, text, music, or program code. The model captures the patterns of the training data and samples new instances with similar characteristics. Generative models usually learn without manual labels, through self-supervised learning (see Experience below). Applications include image synthesis, text generation, style transfer, data augmentation, chatbots, code assistants, assets for games, and summarization. derives conclusions from knowledge with logical techniques such as deduction and induction. Knowledge-based systems, for example expert systems written in Prolog, use facts and rules to prove or disprove statements within a closed world. Machine learning now supports theorem proving and constraint solving, and large language models produce intermediate reasoning steps before an answer, which improves their results on problems that need several steps.

, such as robots and self-driving cars, act in an environment and adjust their behavior to rewards and penalties, which is reinforcement learning (see Experience below). They must decide in situations that their programmers could not anticipate or hard-code. This raises questions of machine ethics: when a collision with an animal or a person is unavoidable, should the car risk an evasive maneuver that endangers its passengers? Liability for mistakes, safety, privacy, and the hacking of vehicles remain open questions for law and society.

The experience is the data that the system observes during training and what it is told about that data. The types of experience differ in the feedback they provide: correct outputs, outputs for some examples only, no outputs, rewards, or outputs taken from the data itself.

A supervised learning algorithm observes a dataset of features together with their targets. It learns a general rule that maps features to targets, so that it can predict the targets of new examples. The term comes from the idea of a teacher who provides the targets and so shows the algorithm how features map to labels.

shows both kinds of targets. The goal is not to reproduce the targets of the training set but to generalize to new data. The teacher therefore usually provides a performance measure along with the labels, which checks how well the rule generalizes.
explains why the two goals differ.
Labels are expensive. Creating them is laborious work, much like producing metadata for a collection (
). This motivates approaches that need fewer labels or none: semi-supervised and self-supervised learning.

In semi-supervised learning, only some training examples have targets. In credit card fraud detection, for example, only the transactions that were investigated carry the label “fraud” or “no fraud”, and the vast majority remains unlabeled. To learn from such data, algorithms make assumptions about how the labels relate to the distribution of the features:
: points close to each other share the same label, so the label changes smoothly across the feature space.
: the data forms clusters, and all objects in a cluster share the same label.
: the features are high-dimensional, but the data lies close to a low-dimensional manifold.
contrasts two ways to use the unlabeled points.

learns a general rule that labels any new point. Its simplest form trains a supervised model on the labeled examples and applies it to the unlabeled ones. This works when only a few labels are missing. When most labels are missing, the labeled part is too small to capture the distribution of the labels, and the approach ignores most of the data.

has a narrower goal: it learns no rule for points that arrive later, but only predicts the labels of the unlabeled points already in the dataset. For this, it uses the positions of all points, labeled and unlabeled, because together they show where the clusters are. A simple partitioning method builds the clusters as follows. It starts with one cluster that contains all objects. While a cluster contains two labeled objects with different labels, it splits the cluster to resolve the conflict. Finally, it gives every unlabeled object the label of the labeled objects in its cluster. Many variants exist for building the clusters.

Unsupervised learning algorithms observe data without targets and derive a function that describes its structure or distribution. No teacher provides targets or evaluates the result; the algorithm must find meaningful patterns on its own.
shows the two most common findings, a cluster and an outlier. Typical tasks are:
: find groups of similar objects based on a distance function. The number of groups is often unknown.
: learn the normal behavior and identify the objects that deviate strongly from it. The training data may itself contain outliers.
: describe the data with a density function, from a single Gaussian to the best fit among several families of distributions.
: extract the core concepts of high-dimensional features, for example with principal component analysis, for a simpler yet accurate view of the data.
: map high-dimensional data onto a two-dimensional grid by competitive learning.

Self-supervised learning takes the targets from the data itself. It hides part of an example and trains the model to predict the hidden part from the rest. No manual labels are needed, so the model can learn from collections with billions of examples. Technically, it is supervised learning with free labels. Several models in this book learn this way. Word2vec predicts the words around a center word (
). BERT masks 15% of the tokens of a sentence and predicts them from the context (
), and generative language models predict the next token. Contrastive learning pairs data from different modalities: CLIP learns that an image and its caption from the web belong together (
). Pairs collected from the web are noisy, so this setting is also called weak supervision.
Learned representations, whether they come from supervised or self-supervised training, serve new tasks with few labels.
trains a classifier on frozen image embeddings with only six labeled photos.
Generative adversarial networks, introduced by Goodfellow and colleagues in 2014, also create their own labels.

shows the two networks. A generator turns random noise into a sample, for example an image. A discriminator receives real samples from the dataset and generated ones and predicts for each whether it is real or generated. The labels “real” and “generated” come for free. The two networks compete: the generator learns to make the discriminator wrong, and the discriminator learns to tell the two kinds of samples apart. Diffusion models have since replaced generative adversarial networks in most image generators.
